verses.translation_literal: Of David. Bless, my soul, [the] YHWH, and all my inward parts [bless] the name of his holiness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Of David. Rise, my soul. Bless the LORD. And every hidden part of me, every depth I cannot see, bless his holy name.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with a man giving orders to himself. David does not address God first; he addresses his own throat-and-breath, his nefesh, and commands it to bless. Hebrew nefesh is the living creature (the neck, the appetite, the self), so this is not a polite note to an invisible soul; the whole person is being called to attention. Because nefesh is grammatically feminine, the imperative is the feminine בָּרֲכִי, a voice you can hear in the long closed vowels. Play it as someone gathering themselves, not performing.

The second line lowers the volume and goes deeper: קְרָבַי, 'my inward parts', is the same word used for entrails in sacrificial texts. The KJV's 'all that is within me' is faithful but pale; the Hebrew is anatomical. Even the guts are to praise. The verb is not repeated, so the actor has to carry the command across the gap. 'Name of his holiness' is a construct chain, not an adjective: the KJV 'his holy name' flattens it. The name stands for the person, who is set apart. 'Bless' here is baraḵ, the verb from which 'knee' (berekh) is likely derived, to kneel and bring gift or praise.

The heading 'of David' is verse 1 in the Hebrew count; the KJV prints it as a title and starts counting afterwards, which is why the verse numbers can look off by one.

philological_notes.note: Not a disembodied 'soul' in the Greek sense: nefesh is the living self, with its throat, breath and appetite. Here it is the speaker's own whole being, spoken to as 'you'. Ibn Ezra reads it as the higher soul (נשמה), Radak as the faculty of wisdom, Rashi through five 'worlds' of a person's life.
'My inward parts': the entrails, the organs inside the body. Radak understands heart and kidneys, or the whole body by figure; Metzudat Zion compares וְקִרְבִּי לְקִיר חֶרֶשׂ (Isa 16:11).

verses.translation_literal: Bless, my soul, [the] YHWH, and do not forget all his repayments.
verses.translation_dramatic: Bless the LORD, my soul. And do not let it slip from you, do not forget one thing he has done for you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first command repeats, but now a second, negative one is attached: do not forget. This is the psalm's real subject. In the Hebrew world memory is not recollection but fidelity; to forget is to stop acting on what you owe. The speaker is talking himself out of ingratitude, so keep the tone gentle and a little urgent, like someone reminding himself of a debt that cannot be paid.

The key word is גְּמוּלָיו, from גָּמַל. The KJV 'benefits' is a decent guess, but the word really means 'what he has paid out', the requital of a deed. Normally it is used of repayment, even punishment; here it is entirely good, and verse 10 will turn the same root around: God has not repaid us according to our iniquities. The echo is a deliberate hinge. Meiri notes that gamal is the language of settling accounts (Joel 4:4).

The KJV, ASV and Webster agree on 'benefits'; the BBE's 'blessings' is looser. 'Forget not' is archaic English for the plain jussive אַל־תִּשְׁכְּחִי, again in the feminine, addressed to the nefesh.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'his repayments', what he has paid out. The root is neutral: it means to deal out a deed in return, for good or ill. Here good; in v. 10 the verb gamal returns for the repayment we have not received.
'Forget' in the Bible is more than losing a fact; it is dropping one's loyalty to it. The jussive is feminine, agreeing with nefesh.

verses.translation_literal: The one forgiving to all your iniquity, the one healing to all your diseases.
verses.translation_dramatic: He is the one who forgives you, every wrong of yours. He is the one who heals you, every sickness that has laid hold of you.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the list of what must not be forgotten begins, and it is built from participles with the article: 'the forgiving one', 'the healing one'. These are not past tenses; they describe what he is, what he does as habit. The KJV 'who forgiveth' captures this, but English needs the relative clause where Hebrew has a title. Each line is a single epithet.

Two things are worth noticing. First, עָוֹן is not just 'a sin'; it is the twisting of a person, and by extension the guilt and punishment that come from it. Second, תַּחֲלֻאִים is a rare plural, 'sicknesses', and it is paired with iniquity. In the ancient Near East illness was commonly read as the consequence of guilt or the work of a hostile power, so the pairing is natural: the same God who clears the account clears the body. Ibn Ezra goes this way, saying that God chastened him with illness to bring him back (he points to Elihu's speeches in Job). Malbim, following Maimonides, reads sin as the soul's disease. Both readings are in the tradition; the text does not choose.

The suffixes עֲוֹנֵכִי and תַּחֲלֻאָיְכִי use an old long form of 'your' (feminine), still addressing the nefesh. Radak, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion all say the extra yod is simply a stylistic flourish. The KJV's 'thine' and 'thy' hide that the addressee is feminine.

philological_notes.note: 'Your iniquity': עָוֹן is guilt as a twist or bend, and by extension its consequence. The long ending -כִי is an archaic spelling of the feminine 'your'.

'Your diseases', a rare plural (also Deut 29:21; Jer 14:18). Paired with iniquity as if sickness and guilt were one thing seen two ways; Radak says the second colon repeats the first with different words, the 'sickness' being that of the soul.

verses.translation_literal: The one redeeming from the pit your life, the one crowning you [with] covenant-loyalty and compassions.
verses.translation_dramatic: He is the one who buys back your life from the pit, the one who sets a crown on your head: steadfast love, and the deep tenderness of a mother's womb.
verses.directors_commentary:
The participles go on. 'Redeems' is גָּאַל, the legal act of the family redeemer, the go'el who buys back a relative from slavery or pays what is owed. The picture is a rescue by someone who has a claim on you by kinship. The 'pit' (שַׁחַת) is the grave, the place where the dead go down; the KJV's 'destruction' softens it into an abstraction. Meiri and Radak hear a death sentence for sin; Targum even reads Gehenna. The play is on the body: you were as good as buried, and he bought you out.

The second half reverses the scene from pit to crown. 'Crowns you' is a participle with a suffix, מְעַטְּרֵכִי, built from עֲטָרָה, a wreath or diadem. What he places on the head is not gold but two things: חֶסֶד, covenant-loyalty (the KJV 'lovingkindness' is Coverdale's coinage, and more affectionate than the legal weight the word carries), and רַחֲמִים, a plural of 'compassion' built on the word for womb (רֶחֶם). The KJV's 'tender mercies' is closer than the BBE's 'grace'. Say the plural: it is an accumulation of acts of tenderness, not an abstraction.

The long suffix -כִי again: the extra yod is the old feminine ending, with Meiri noting several parallels in the Psalms (116:7).

philological_notes.note: The family redeemer: the kinsman who buys back a person or property (Lev 25; Ruth). Used of God as the nearest relative who pays the price.

The pit, the grave. Some derive it from שׁוּחַ 'to sink', others from שָׁחַת 'to destroy', which is why older versions say 'destruction'. Meiri takes it as the grave or the loss of the soul; Radak as eternal loss.
Compassions: the plural of an abstract noun from רֶחֶם, womb. The tenderness of a parent's body, not of a judge.

verses.translation_literal: The one satisfying with the good your ornament; it renews itself like the eagle, your youth.
verses.translation_dramatic: He is the one who fills you to the full with good things, until what adorns you is satisfied. And then it happens: your youth shakes itself new, like an eagle lifting out of its old feathers, wings wide to the morning.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play the first half as a table laid after a long illness. The verb is from the root of fullness, the same word a hungry throat uses, and the object is the puzzle: עֶדְיֵךְ, literally 'your ornament'. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all read it as 'your mouth', on the strength of Psalm 32:9, where the same word means the trappings of a horse's head, the bit and bridle. For them the picture is a sick person whose mouth had turned from every food, now filled with good things alongside returning health (Radak and Meiri on Psalm 103:5). Ibn Ezra reports that reading, 'your mouth', but gives his own: the soul is the ornament of the body, so the verse means 'who satisfies your soul with good', answering the cry 'my soul is satisfied' of Psalm 63:6. Either way the psalm turns from forgiveness to the body's recovery, and the audience should feel both.

The KJV 'thy mouth' adopts the first reading without telling you that the Hebrew says 'ornament', and its 'so that thy youth is renewed' invents a purpose clause the Hebrew does not have: the verse simply sets two clauses side by side, with no 'so that'. The second half also breaks grammar on purpose. 'Youth' is a plural noun with the feminine 'your', and the verb is feminine singular: 'it renews itself'. Meiri observes that the word is written without a letter one might expect, and that 'soul', addressed in this psalm as 'you', can take either gender. The eagle is a figure of vigor in Isaiah 40:31 as well. Rashi says it is the eagle that renews wing and feather year by year, and adds an aggadah (Genesis Rabbah 19:5) of an eagle that becomes young again in old age; Radak and Meiri report a longer legend of a ten-year cycle. Do not play the legend: the psalm needs only the image of a bird heavy with age that rises light.

philological_notes.note: From עֲדִי 'ornament, finery'. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion read it as 'your mouth', comparing 'its ornament (עדיו) is bit and bridle' in Psalm 32:9, where the word names the horse's gear. Ibn Ezra reports 'mouth' but prefers the soul as the body's ornament: 'who satisfies your soul with good'. The KJV, ASV and BBE all choose 'mouth' or 'desire'; the Hebrew states neither.

'Your youth', with the long feminine ending -ekhi, an old form of 'your' addressed to the soul. The plural abstract (youth, as a time of life) takes the feminine singular verb 'it renews itself', as Radak notes of the feminine form of the verb.

verses.translation_literal: Doing righteousnesses, YHWH, and judgments for all [who are] oppressed.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is a doer of righteous deeds, and where the crushed are, he brings judgments: a verdict, and another, for every last one who is oppressed.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm steps out of the first person. The singer has been thanking God for his own healing; now the voice widens to the whole of God's dealing, and the actors should widen with it, as if the room had opened. Radak connects the two: because God had dealt kindly with the sick man, the psalmist says this is simply how God deals with all his creatures. The participle 'doing' is ongoing, not a single event, and both nouns are plural, 'righteousnesses' and 'judgments': a long line of acts, not a principle.

The KJV 'executeth righteousness and judgment' flattens both plurals into abstractions and uses a courtroom verb, 'executeth', that now suggests an execution. The Hebrew is the plain 'does', and what it does is concrete. The word עֲשׁוּקִים is the oppressed, those defrauded or squeezed by someone stronger: its root is the same as for the withheld wages of a day-laborer. Meiri reads it as justice that rescues the oppressed from the hand of the oppressor. Malbim sees the verse dividing God's response: righteousness shown to the sinner, but justice kept for wrongs between one person and another, where repentance is of no use until the stolen thing is returned. Radak takes the lamed of 'for all' as 'for the sake of', and 'all' as the oppressed of whatever nation, so the verse does not stop at Israel's border.

philological_notes.note: A plural: 'righteous acts' or 'acts of vindication', as in Judges 5:11, rather than the abstract 'righteousness' of the KJV. Ibn Ezra connects it with the preceding diseases: God is righteous in all his ways even in affliction.

A passive participle, 'those who are oppressed, defrauded'. Metzudat Zion glosses the root as 'oppression and robbery'. Meiri takes the verse to mean that God rescues the oppressed from the oppressor.

verses.translation_literal: He makes known his ways to Moses, to the sons of Israel his deeds.
verses.translation_dramatic: He made his ways known to Moses. To the people of Israel he showed his deeds.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm now looks at history, and the tense changes. 'He makes known' is a yiqtol, an imperfect (Ibn Ezra says it stands for the past, as in 'they make a calf in Horeb', Ps 106:19). The KJV's 'made known' is a fair reading. The scene is Sinai: Moses asks 'let me know your ways' (Exod 33:13) and the answer is the list of divine attributes that verse 8 will recite.

A fine point: 'ways' (דְּרָכִים) and 'deeds' (עֲלִילוֹת) are not the same. Ways are the settled character, the road God walks by; deeds are the particular things he has done, as in the plagues and the wilderness. Moses gets the road, Israel the events. That is the parallelism, although many modern translators treat them as synonyms; Malbim presses the difference, and the KJV 'acts' is appropriate. Play the distinction: one is learned in private on a mountain, the other seen in public by a whole people.

In the ancient world gods were known by their deeds on behalf of a nation, not by teachings. This line says that Israel's God also has a character that could be told, and was told to one man.

philological_notes.note: 'His ways': the road, the manner of conduct. Radak connects it with Moses's request in Exod 33:13 and the thirteen attributes, which verse 8 quotes.
'His deeds, his doings'; the word usually describes deeds that are notable, public or dramatic (Ps 9:12). Malbim separates it from 'ways' as an act proceeding from a disposition.

verses.translation_literal: Compassionate and gracious [is] YHWH, long of nostrils and great of covenant-loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Compassionate and gracious is the LORD. Slow to burn, and rich beyond counting in steadfast love.
verses.directors_commentary:
These are the words God spoke to Moses on the mountain (Exod 34:6), here turned into a hymn. The Hebrew is almost a creed: four attributes, in a fixed order, which the Bible quotes again and again (Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2, Neh 9:17, Ps 86:15). As Ibn Ezra and Meiri note, David quotes only part of the thirteen: he omits 'truth' and keeps what a sick and sinful person needs.

The Hebrew idiom for patience is אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם, literally 'long of nostrils'. Anger in Hebrew is a snorting, a burning in the nose (אַף means both 'nose' and 'anger'), and being 'long' of it means the fire takes a long time to reach you. The KJV's 'slow to anger' is faithful in sense but drops the body; the dual form 'nostrils' is part of the picture. Keep it vivid for the actor: a breath that is held, not released.

רַחוּם comes from רֶחֶם, the womb, so 'merciful' hides a mother's compassion. חַנּוּן, 'gracious', is favor freely given to someone who has no claim. And חֶסֶד, once more, is covenant loyalty: the KJV 'plenteous in mercy' is a rendering of Coverdale's 'lovingkindness' elsewhere, but here it says 'mercy', reusing a word that also translates רַחֲמִים. Two different Hebrew words, one English, so the double is lost.

philological_notes.note: Idiom for patience: 'long of nostrils'. The dual of אַף is used for the face or nose, and anger shows in the nose. The opposite is 'short of spirit' (Prov 14:29). Radak explains it as God delaying the punishment in the hope that we will return.
'Compassionate', from רֶחֶם 'womb'. Used only of God in the Bible. Radak explains it as God's compassion for his people in exile.
Loyalty within a relationship, kindness that a covenant partner owes and gives beyond what is owed. Ibn Ezra reads 'great of ḥesed' as the promise that it will never stop.

verses.translation_literal: Not to perpetuity will he contend, and not for ever will he keep.
verses.translation_dramatic: He will not contend forever. He will not nurse his grudge for all time.
verses.directors_commentary:
The two verbs here come from the language of the lawsuit and the grudge. יָרִיב, from רִיב, is to bring a case, to press a legal charge against someone; it is more than 'chide', which the KJV chose and which has the sound of a nurse scolding a child. The ASV and Webster repeat it. The BBE's 'bitter feeling' misses that this is a courtroom action. God can conduct a case against his people; the verse says he does not do it for ever.

יִטּוֹר, from נָטַר, 'to keep, to guard', is what a person does with a hatred: he keeps it, guards it, waits for the day. The KJV supplies 'his anger' (the Hebrew leaves the object out), which is reasonable, since Lev 19:18 uses it in 'you shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge' (Metzudat Zion cites that). The pair 'to perpetuity' (לָנֶצַח) and 'for ever' (לְעוֹלָם) are near synonyms, though Malbim presses a difference. Radak and Meiri read the verse as hope for return from exile; Ibn Ezra, more carefully, says it is about those who return.

Be careful with the sense: the text says he will not do it for ever, which allows for a period of the case being pressed. This is a promise with limits, not a denial of divine anger.

philological_notes.note: To bring or conduct a dispute or lawsuit. The noun rib is a legal quarrel, and the prophets use it for God's case against Israel (Hos 4:1; Mic 6:2).
To keep, guard; with a grudge, to hold on to anger. Metzudat Zion connects it with Lev 19:18, 'you shall not take revenge or keep a grudge'.

verses.translation_literal: Not according to our sins has he done to us, and not according to our iniquities has he repaid upon us.
verses.translation_dramatic: He has not treated us as our sins deserve. He has not paid us back by the weight of our wrongs.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker has moved from 'you' to 'us': the whole community now stands inside the psalm. The line is a double negation set in perfect tenses, a fact of experience: he has not done, he has not repaid. Ancient Near Eastern thinking about gods and law was usually the reverse: sin demands payment, and the gods keep strict books. This verse says the books were not balanced.

Two roots carry the verse. חֵטְא and עָוֹן are not interchangeable: sin (a missing of the mark) and iniquity (a twist, with its guilt). Malbim insists on the difference, which most translations erase. And גָּמַל returns from verse 2: there it described the good he has paid out; here it is the payment we did not get. The KJV's 'dealt with' and 'rewarded' use two different English words for עָשָׂה and גָּמַל, and 'rewarded' is a euphemism, since gamal here means repaid in kind, and the repayment would have been punishment. The BBE spells that out as 'punishment' and 'reward'.

Play it as astonished confession, not as a theological proposition. Ibn Ezra notes that David includes others with himself: the God who forgives all includes the whole group.

philological_notes.note: To deal out in return, repay, whether good or ill. It returns from the 'repayments' of v. 2; here the repayment withheld is the punishment. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'payment of wages'.

'Our sins' and 'our iniquities' are a poetic pair, but Malbim distinguishes them: sin as error or passion, iniquity as deliberate perversion. Radak says the verse repeats one idea in two sets of words.

verses.translation_literal: For as the height of heavens above the earth, his covenant-loyalty is mighty over those fearing him.
verses.translation_dramatic: For as high as the heavens stand above the earth, so mighty is his steadfast love toward those who fear him.
verses.directors_commentary:
'For' (כִּי) gives the reason for the last verse. How do we know he has not repaid us? Because his loyalty is measured by the height of the sky. The Hebrew compares with the idiom כִּגְבֹהַּ, 'as the height of', and the verb גָּבַר, 'to be mighty, to prevail', is then used of חֶסֶד: love has the upper hand. The KJV's 'so great is his mercy' keeps the comparison but loses the verb of strength, a military word (the root of gibbor, 'warrior'): the loyalty wins.

The measure is deliberately not a measure. A farmer or shepherd in Judah, looking up at the sky, knew that there was nothing higher; the sky was a solid vault. Ibn Ezra and Radak both say that nothing looks higher to the human eye. Malbim presses the logic: it is not that God's mercy is a little greater than our worth, but that there is no proportion at all between them.

'Those who fear him' (יְרֵאָיו) are not the terrified. It is the standard biblical term for people who stand in awe of God and keep faith with him. Radak makes the point that it means Israel, since even when they sin, they return. The KJV 'them that fear him' is accurate; the BBE's 'worshippers' narrows it to ritual.

philological_notes.note: To be strong, to prevail (the root of gever, gibbor 'mighty man'). Of ḥesed it means that loyalty prevails over; the KJV 'great' weakens it. Malbim reads it as a pure gift, out of all proportion to merit.
'Those fearing him', i.e. those who revere him and keep covenant; Radak says it is Israel as a whole, who may sin but return.

verses.translation_literal: As the distance of east from west, he has made far from us our transgressions.
verses.translation_dramatic: As far as the sunrise lies from the sunset, so far has he carried our rebellions away from us.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse gives a second image of measure, now horizontal: not height, but distance. The Hebrew word 'east' (מִזְרָח) is 'where the sun shines forth', and 'west' (מַעֲרָב) is where it goes in, where evening comes. They are the farthest apart a person can think, and they never meet; the lines of the compass have no touching point. The KJV 'as far as the east is from the west' is correct, and one of the most famous lines of the Psalms. Notice that the Hebrew uses a noun, 'the distance of', where English uses 'as far as'.

Radak asks why east and west, and not north and south. His answer: the inhabited world runs east to west, and no one can travel from north to south because of cold or heat; it is the longest measure people actually know. That is an ancient geographic explanation and not in the text.

The real force is in the verb: הִרְחִיק, the causative of 'to be far'. He has 'made them far', an action, not a pardon. And the thing removed is פְּשָׁעֵינוּ, 'our transgressions', which means rebellion, a breach of covenant, the strongest of the three words for wrongdoing in this passage; the KJV 'transgressions' fits. Tradition distinguishes the three terms (sin, iniquity, rebellion), but here all are taken away.

philological_notes.note: Causative: 'he has made far, removed'. The same root appears in the first colon, כִּרְחֹק, 'as the distance of', so the measure and the deed share a root. Ibn Ezra says he does it again every time we return.

Rebellion, deliberate breach of a relationship, the political word for a vassal's revolt (1 Kgs 12:19, of the northern tribes against the house of David). The third of the three words for wrongdoing the psalm has used (iniquity v. 3, sin v. 10).

verses.translation_literal: Like the compassion of a father on [his] sons, YHWH has compassion on those who fear him.
verses.translation_dramatic: As a father bends over his children and his heart goes soft toward them, so the LORD bends toward those who stand in awe of him, and his heart goes soft.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is built on one root said twice: a father has *racham*, and YHWH has *racham*. Say the two halves as one breath, because the point is that the second compassion is the same thing as the first. The KJV's "pitieth" is the weak spot. It makes God look down on his children from a height, as one pities the unfortunate. *Racham* is the tenderness that comes from the womb (*rechem*), the felt, bodily pull a parent has toward a child. It is closer to "has the guts for them". There is also an irony in the setting: in a household of the ancient Near East the father is the one with the legal power of life and death over his sons, so his compassion is a choice made from strength, not a reflex of the weak. Note too that *banim* is "sons", the word that also serves for "children", and the KJV's "children" is a fair widening. "Those who fear him" (*yere'av*) is not terror; in the Psalms it is the posture of the loyal subject, and the next verses define it as keeping the covenant. Radak says there is no mercy greater than the father's for the son.

philological_notes.note: The verb 'to have compassion', repeated from the infinitive 'like the compassion of' in the first half. The noun רֶחֶם is 'womb', and the root carries that sense of tender, bodily feeling. English 'pity' loses both the repetition and the womb image.
'Those who fear him': an active participle with a suffix. The fear in view is reverent loyalty, which v. 17 and v. 18 spell out as keeping the covenant.

verses.translation_literal: For he, he knows our formation; [he is] remembering that we [are] dust.
verses.translation_dramatic: For he knows how we were shaped. He knows what we were shaped from, and he has not forgotten it: we are dust.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the reason behind the compassion of v. 13: *ki*, "for". The KJV's "frame" is an old word for a built structure and hides the Hebrew picture. *Yetzer* comes from *yatzar*, "to form", the verb used of a potter working clay, and for God forming the man "dust from the ground" in Genesis 2:7. So "our formation" is "what we were molded out of", and the Psalmist ends on the same material: *afar*, dust. The two halves are one thought said twice, as Radak and Metzudat David both observe: to know the formation is to remember the dust. *Zakhur* is a passive adjective, "remembered", so Rashi and the Targum read it as "it is kept in remembrance before him", that is, God does not let it slip. Later Jewish readers (the Targum, Meiri, Radak) take *yetzer* as the inclination to evil, from Genesis 8:21, and the Targum makes this explicit with "our evil inclination". The Hebrew itself says only "what we are made of", and I would not play the inclination over the word on stage. The dust is not an insult. It is the ground on which mercy stands.

philological_notes.note: 'Our formation', from the verb 'to form' used of the potter and of the creation of man (Gen 2:7). The Targum renders it 'our evil inclination'; the Hebrew says only what we are formed from.
A passive adjective: 'remembered' or 'kept in mind'. Radak says it means the same as 'he knows': it is always before him.

verses.translation_literal: Mortal man: like grass [are] his days; like the flower of the field, so he blossoms.
verses.translation_dramatic: A man, a mortal. His days are grass. He blossoms the way a flower of the open field blossoms, and no differently.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse opens with a bare word, *enosh*, set apart from the rest: "Mortal man, his days are like grass." *Enosh* is the word for the human being in his weakness, not *adam* (the one from *adamah*, earth) and not *ish* (the man of standing). The KJV's "As for man" is a fair stand-in, but it loses that this is the frail word. Two images follow, both from the Judean landscape. *Chatzir* is grass that springs after the winter rains and, as Metzudat David notes, dries fast in the heat of the sun. The "flower of the field" is a wild one, not a garden plant: nobody waters it. Hear the sounds: *chatzir*, *tzitz*, *yatzitz*. The noun for the flower and the verb "blossoms" are the same root, so the line hisses and flickers. The KJV's "flourisheth" sounds like thriving for years; the verb is the quick burst of one flower. Radak and the Targum agree that the point is brevity, not beauty.

philological_notes.note: The 'mortal' or frail human being, as against אָדָם. The standing connection with weakness is the sense of the root.
'He blossoms': the verb has the same root as the noun צִיץ 'flower' just before it, so English 'flower ... flowers' would be nearer than 'flower ... flourishes'.

verses.translation_literal: For a wind has passed over him, and he is not; and his place will not recognize him again.
verses.translation_dramatic: A wind goes over him, only a wind, and he is gone. And the place where he stood looks and does not know him any more.
verses.directors_commentary: The *ki*, "for", ties this to the flower: this is how the flower goes. The wind in question is the *ruach*, in the hot season the dry east wind that comes off the desert and scorches the hills. Isaiah 40:7 uses the same image: grass withers "because the breath (*ruach*) of the LORD blows on it". Here the word is bare, "a wind", and the KJV's "passeth over it" fixes the pronoun on the flower. The Hebrew has only "over him" (*bo*), a masculine suffix with no named referent, so it can be the flower and the man together, and the verse walks from one to the other. The second half is the sharper blow. "His place" does not recognize him: the very ground he occupied (*meqomo*) is given a face and a memory, and it has none. The KJV's "shall know it no more" is the right sense in older words. This is a statement about being forgotten by the world, not about death as pain. Rashi reads *ruach* as an illness, a mortal sickness passing through; Metzudat David, as a small breath of divine anger. Pick the reading you like; the actor's job is to let the line be small and final.

philological_notes.note: 'And he is not': the particle of non-existence with a suffix. It is the plain word for 'is gone', with no verb of dying.
'It will recognize him': the verb for recognizing a person or taking note of him. The subject is 'his place', so the place itself fails to know him.

verses.translation_literal: And the covenant loyalty of YHWH [is] from forever and until forever upon those who fear him, and his righteousness to the sons of sons,
verses.translation_dramatic: But the LORD's faithful love has no beginning we can point to and no end. It rests on those who fear him, and his justice runs down to their children's children.
verses.directors_commentary: The *ve* at the start is a turn, "but": after the wind and the forgotten place, a love that does not blow away. *Chesed* is the hardest word in the verse. The KJV's "mercy" is the standard choice, but it makes the word sound like pardon for wrongdoing. *Chesed* is loyalty owed inside a bond: what a partner in a covenant does because the bond holds, even when he need not. Hence "covenant loyalty", and v. 18 names the covenant at once. *Me'olam ve'ad olam*, "from forever to forever", has the same word at both ends; the KJV's "from everlasting to everlasting" gets this. *Olam* is an unmeasured long time, and Radak, Metzudat David and the Targum take it as a reach from this world into the next (the Targum says "from this world to the world to come"). *Tzidqato* is "his righteousness", and in the Psalms this means the faithful acting of the one who keeps his word to the people he is bound to, not an abstract justice. "Sons of sons" is the Hebrew idiom for grandchildren and on, three generations that stand for all. Radak adds that it need not be the third generation exactly.

philological_notes.note: Loyalty within a relationship of obligation; 'mercy' and 'lovingkindness' are the usual English renderings, and each loses the covenant sense. Radak says it is the surplus of good beyond what was owed.
'To the sons of sons': the idiom for grandchildren, standing for all later generations. Radak says it is not only the third generation.

verses.translation_literal: To those who keep his covenant, and to those who remember his precepts, to do them.
verses.translation_dramatic: To those who keep his covenant, who carry his commands in mind in order to do them.
verses.directors_commentary: This verse sets the condition for the promise of v. 17, and it is the sentence that stops "those who fear him" from sounding like a family right. The "children's children" are included only as they keep the covenant. Read it as a hinge. "Keep" (*shomrei*) and "remember" (*zokhrei*) go together: one is guarding, the other is holding in mind, and the last phrase, *la'asotam*, "to do them", says that remembering is meant to end in action. Radak makes the point: learning without doing is worthless. The KJV's "commandments" turns *piqqudim* into the common word for commands; the term is rarer, a word of the Psalms for "precepts" or "charges", given by an overseer to those under him (from the root *paqad*, to oversee). "Remember" in Hebrew is active and often means "to act on", so the KJV's "that remember" is better than BBE's "have in mind". The Hebrew gives no "if", though BBE adds one; the condition is carried by the participles.

philological_notes.note: 'His precepts': a word found almost only in the Psalms (especially Ps 119) for the charges of God. It is related to the verb 'to appoint, oversee'.
'To do them': the purpose of the remembering. Radak: remembering by mouth and study is not enough without doing.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH in the heavens has established his throne, and his kingdom has ruled over the all.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD has set his throne firm in the heavens, and his kingdom rules over everything there is.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm lifts its eyes: from dust and wind to a throne. *Hekhin*, "has established", is the verb for making firm and fixed, not the KJV's "prepared", which suggests a seat made ready for a guest who has not come. This throne is set and it stays. The word order puts "YHWH" first, then "in the heavens": it is YHWH, as against the shifting grass, whose seat is stable. The kingdom has "ruled over the all", *bakol*, "over everything". The verb *mashalah* is a completed action that stands for a continuing rule: the kingdom has been ruling and still is. For a first audience the polemic is in the place: the great throne was a thing of Near Eastern palaces and temples, and the surrounding peoples set their gods' thrones in particular cities and on particular mountains. Here one throne is in the heavens and its rule has no local limits, which is also the point of v. 22. Radak says that if the heavens are his throne, then everything is beneath his feet.

philological_notes.note: 'He has established': the causative of a root meaning 'to be firm'. It describes setting something on a firm base, not preparing it for later use.
'Has ruled': a perfect verb used for a rule that has been exercised and still is. Rashi glosses it with the participle 'rules'.

verses.translation_literal: Bless YHWH, his messengers, mighty ones of strength, doers of his word, by listening to the voice of his word.
verses.translation_dramatic: Bless the LORD, you who are his messengers, you mighty ones, strong beyond measure. You carry out his word, and you listen for the very sound of it.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm now calls on those who already stand at the throne. *Mal'akhav* is "his messengers". The KJV's "angels" is a Greek-derived word, *angelos*, with a long Christian history of wings and halos behind it; the Hebrew names a job, one who is sent, and the same word is used of human envoys. These are heavenly beings, yet it is their role the text stresses. "Mighty ones of strength" is a doubling (*gibborei koach*), the strongest Hebrew way to say "warriors": the KJV's "that excel in strength" is a mild version. The verse is built on a nice reversal. In ordinary life one hears first, then does. Here the messengers are "doers" of the word first and "listeners" second, a point Meiri records from the old homilies: they act before they have heard, as Israel said "we will do" before "we will hear" at Sinai. The KJV breaks the echo: it renders the same word *davar* as "commandments" and then as "word". Keep "word" twice. Ibn Ezra reads the last line as the angels' own reward: for them, hearing the voice is itself the pleasure, not a path to wages.

philological_notes.note: 'His messengers': from a root meaning 'to send'. The word names the role of the one sent, and is used of human envoys as well as heavenly beings.
'His word': it stands twice in the verse (עֹשֵׂי דְבָרוֹ, בְּקוֹל דְּבָרוֹ). The KJV varies it; the echo is part of the sense, 'doing the word by hearing the word'.

verses.translation_literal: Bless YHWH, all his hosts, his attendants, doers of his will.
verses.translation_dramatic: Bless the LORD, all you who are his armies, you who wait on him, who do what he wills.
verses.directors_commentary: The call widens: from the "mighty ones" to *kol tzeva'av*, "all his hosts". *Tzava* is the word for an army, a mustered force, and the same word is behind "the LORD of hosts" (YHWH *tzeva'ot*): the armies of heaven. The KJV's "hosts" is right but now sounds like a crowd of guests, and "ye ministers" now suggests clergy. *Meshartav* are attendants, those who serve a master in person, as Joshua served Moses and Elisha served Elijah; the same root is used for the service of priests. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read the hosts as the stars and heavenly bodies, the "host of heaven", which is a possible sense of *tzava* (Deut 4:19), and fits the polemic: what the nations worshipped as gods are here only soldiers of one king. The last phrase, *oseh retzono*, "doing his will", replaces the "word" of v. 20 with "will", moving from the spoken order to the wish that has not been spoken. The KJV's "pleasure" is archaic: it means what he wants, not what he enjoys.

philological_notes.note: 'His hosts': armies or a mustered force; also the 'host of heaven', the stars and heavenly beings. The commentators read it either way.
'His attendants': those who serve a master in person, a word also used for priestly service.

verses.translation_literal: Bless YHWH, all his works, in all the places of his dominion. Bless, my self, YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Bless the LORD, all that he has made, in every place his rule reaches. And you, my soul, bless the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary: The circle closes. The first call (v. 20) went to the beings at the throne, the second (v. 21) to the armies, and now the third goes to *kol ma'asav*, "all his works", everything that exists, "in all the places of his dominion". Notice the repeated *kol*, "all", three times in this verse and the verse before it: nothing is outside the call. Then the voice drops to one person: *bar'khi nafshi et YHWH*, "Bless, my self, YHWH", the same words that opened the psalm in v. 1. The KJV's "O my soul" carries a Greek idea of an immaterial soul. *Nefesh* is the living self, in its first sense the throat, the breath, the whole person that needs and wants. The imperative *barakhi* is feminine singular because *nefesh* is a grammatically feminine noun. The whole cosmos has been summoned, and at the end the singer takes his place in the chorus. Radak and Meiri note the ring: the psalm ends where it began, because man in his own self gathers heaven and earth together. Play the last line quietly, as a man who has just spoken to the universe turning to himself.

philological_notes.note: 'My self' (traditionally 'my soul'): the living person, with the breath and appetite of the whole self, not a soul apart from the body. The imperative before it is feminine to agree with the noun.
'His dominion': from the same root as the verb in v. 19, 'has ruled'. The two verses frame the rule of God: his throne in v. 19, the extent of his rule here.
